html:
A group of young painters formed in Bombay in 1947, the year of independence, who set out to create a modern Indian art. Its founders included F. N. Souza, S. H. Raza, M. F. Husain, K. H. Ara, H. A. Gade and S. K. Bakre.

They rejected both the academic realism of the colonial art schools, in the line of Raja Ravi Varma, and the gentle revivalism of the Bengal School. Instead they took up the bold forms of European modernism, from Cézanne and Picasso to Expressionism, and mixed them with Indian folk art, temple sculpture and miniature painting. The group had no single style; what joined them was the freedom to experiment.

It lasted only a few years as a group. Souza and Raza moved to Europe, and others went their own ways. But its members became the most famous Indian artists of the 20th century, and in the 2000s their works began to sell for record prices. Husain later lived in exile after attacks over his images of Hindu goddesses. The group marks the start of modern art in independent India, in the decade of Partition.
